summary: Works out, with a contribution from Butler Lampson, how much network capacity a single keystroke uses when a West Coast TIP user is logged in to an East Coast Host. It counts the packets for the character, its acknowledgments, and the echo coming back.

plainLanguage.summary: This note estimates how much network traffic a cross-country keystroke and its returned echo create. It suggests that this traffic may help explain bursts of slow response.

subtitle: A packet-count estimate for a cross-country key press and its echoed character.

tldr.problem: Cross-country users typing through a TIP could experience poor echo response, at least in bursts.
tldr.mechanism: The note counts the messages involved in sending a character and returning its echo, then compares that traffic with the stated cross-country line capacity.
tldr.outcome: The author suggests that network peak loads may explain the delay and that remote echoing in a proposed Telnet protocol could affect network operation. The unit metadata says RFC 568 updates this note.

today: The unit metadata says RFC 567 is updated by RFC 568. This note is an estimate about ARPANET traffic and makes no claim about present-day network performance.

sections.title: Messages Triggered by a Keystroke
sections.content:
The note presents a calculation contributed by Butler Lampson. It considers a West Coast user at a Terminal Interface Processor (TIP) connected to an East Coast host.

For a key press, the TIP sends a one-character message, the destination IMP sends a Request for Next Message (RFNM), the destination host sends an allocation message, and the TIP sends an RFNM for that allocation. The same sequence repeats with the roles reversed for the echoed character.
sections.plainLanguage: A key press triggers several network messages. The character's echo triggers another exchange in the opposite direction.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Estimate
sections.content:
The authors count the exchange as 4 packets or 4000 bits in each direction. They state that cross-country ARPANET capacity is provided by 3 50Kb phone lines and calculate a capacity of 37.5 such characters per second.

The note says that sending RFNMs between IMPs more efficiently could at best double that capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: The estimate compares the bits used by one key-and-echo exchange with the capacity of the cross-country lines. Under those assumptions, the network can handle 37.5 such characters each second.

sections.title: Possible Cause of Slow Echo
sections.content:
The author says the calculation may help explain why cross-country TIP users, including the West Coast community of BBN-TENEX users, experience poor echo response in bursts. The network itself may be undergoing momentary peak loads.

If the argument is correct, the proposed remote-echoing facilities of the new Telnet protocol could have a major effect on network operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The note proposes that short periods of heavy network traffic may make typing responses slow. It says a proposed Telnet remote-echo feature could change how much traffic crosses the network.
